source.title: Scaling Video Generation for Reasoning: At What Cost?
source.authors: Wei-Hang Guo; Xiao-Yu Wu; Yi-Fei Wang; Niloofar Mireshghallah; Lydia E. Kavraki

page_placements.theme: Architecture shape and component allocation affect downstream quality

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The study scales video diffusion transformers and measures held-out flow loss and task accuracy, extending scaling questions beyond text pretraining to video generation.
record.gate_note: The study reports that validation flow MSE follows an approximate power law as model size and training data increase, and that lower MSE does not reliably indicate better state reasoning across models. The plotted MSE curves do not provide extractable point values in the text. Accuracy-by-action, symbolic-guidance, and vector-state results are omitted unless they bear on the tested scaling or predictability versions. Results cited from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study trains video diffusion transformers (20M–1B) from scratch, one epoch, on synthetic Rubik's Cube videos. It reports that validation flow MSE scales roughly as a power law (V5), and it tests whether loss and scale predict downstream state-prediction accuracy (V6). A Stage-A comparison at ~95M parameters gives loss across depth–width shapes (V4, in a non-language system). It is not an original source.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. Validation MSE scales approximately as a power law but does not rank state-reasoning accuracy across model sizes. Smaller models win at low compute, while larger models reach higher accuracy with more training. Accuracy-frontier extrapolations are window-dependent and illustrative. Additions: training gives diminishing returns at fixed size, and symbolic state supervision raises 20M frame accuracy from 31.1% to 67.3% at matched data.
record.recipe_differences: Video diffusion transformers trained from scratch with rectified flow on synthetic Rubik’s Cube videos; the study varies model size, data exposure, and compute rather than language-model parameters, tokens, and text-pretraining loss.
record.method_sensitivity: The study reports that validation MSE does not reliably rank reasoning accuracy across model sizes. Accuracy-frontier 98% compute projections vary substantially between middle-third and final-third fits. Architecture-calibration losses use different conditioning and probes and are declared not directly comparable.

fits_no_version.finding: At ~95M parameters, depth–width shape changes downstream frame accuracy hugely even where loss barely changes (AR-k=1: 3.67% deep-narrow vs 37.22% wide-shallow).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Architecture shape can matter strongly for downstream capability at fixed parameter count, even when the loss difference is small.

fits_no_version.finding: At fixed compute (~0.1 PF-days), the 70M model reaches 44.6% frame accuracy vs 0.3% for the 1B model, which reaches 83.7% at 3.14 PF-days.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The compute-optimal model size for downstream accuracy shifts upward with budget.

record.problems: Validation MSE scaling values and curves are shown in figures without extractable numerical points; no MSE fit coefficients or explicit extrapolation tests for loss are reported. The architecture-calibration losses are not directly comparable across prediction factorizations. Reasoning evaluation uses 100 paired episodes for the principal scaling comparisons, and the accuracy-frontier compute intersections are explicitly described as illustrative, not validated predictions.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted action/sticker/frame accuracy-by-action curves and the symbolic-guidance and vector-state experiments because they do not directly test the versions recorded here. The Stage-A action, sticker, and frame metrics are not loss results; the relevant Stage-A flow-MSE results are recorded in S1–S9.

untested.parts: Language-model pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute is not studied.
No test of whether small-run loss fits predict larger runs. The extrapolations are of accuracy and are not validated.
No compute-optimal parameter/data allocation is estimated. Stage B uses a constant learning rate and an 8M-video cap.
Window-dependence is shown for accuracy-frontier fits only, not for loss exponents or the compute-optimal split.
Only synthetic single-task video; no image, repeated-data, fine-tuning or transfer settings. No loss-fit coefficients are reported.
One synthetic task. No standard downstream benchmarks.

missing.what: Frame accuracy by model size at 5M videos, free-running vs GT-prefix (33.89→71.00% free; A9 frame 0→10%)
Fixed-compute comparison: at ~0.1 PF-days, 70M gets 44.6% vs 1B 0.3%; the 1B model reaches 83.7% at 3.14 PF-days
Within each model, lower MSE generally accompanies higher accuracy
Diminishing returns at fixed size: 120M AR frame accuracy goes from 48.11% to 49.33% between 5M and 8M videos

record.verdict_notes: V4 is linked even though the system is a video DiT, not a language model; researchers may prefer to treat S1–S9 as V5-adjacent. The reader's 'not comparable' note applies across factorizations only, not across shapes. Stage-A shape losses come from a single 1M-video endpoint and a single seed. M1–M14 rest on one sentence plus figures, with no extractable values.

versions.untested_parts: The study uses video generators rather than language models and does not test held-out language-model pretraining loss against parameter count, tokens, or compute.
It does not test whether small-run fits predict the held-out loss of much larger runs.
It does not estimate a loss-minimising parameter/token allocation at fixed compute.

The study compares a limited set of approximately 95M-parameter configurations, but states that their flow-loss probes and conditioning differ and the losses are not directly comparable; it does not establish the effect of architecture on comparable loss.
It tests video generation only, with synthetic Rubik’s Cube data and rectified-flow training; it does not test image or other modalities, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The measured task is Rubik’s Cube state prediction in generated video, not a broad set of downstream tasks or language-model pretraining loss.
The fitting-window analysis concerns task-accuracy compute frontiers, not loss-scaling exponents or a compute-optimal parameter/token split.

statements.correction: Table 10: AR-k=4 maximum-to-minimum MSE increase approximately 8.06%; Bidir approximately 7.60%. These percentages use the minimum loss within each factorization as denominator.
